title: Context: Modern Britain, Masculinity & Identity
content_html:
Malorie Blackman and Boys Don’t Cry

Malorie Blackman is one of Britain’s most important contemporary authors. As Children’s Laureate (2013–2015), she championed diversity in children’s literature, arguing that young people deserve to see themselves reflected in the books they read. Boys Don’t Cry, published in 2010, tackles gender expectations, teen parenthood, homophobia and family under pressure — all set in contemporary Britain. Blackman writes from a position of lived experience as a Black British woman, and her fiction consistently challenges the prejudices that hold young people back.

Key Fact

Blackman said: “I want my readers to feel that anything is possible.” Her fiction consistently features Black British characters in situations where race is present but not the sole defining issue — a deliberate authorial choice to normalise diverse representation.

The Novel’s Setting: Modern Britain

Boys Don’t Cry is set in contemporary urban Britain. The exact city is never named, but the setting reflects the realities of many British families: council estates, stretched finances, single-parent households and the pressure on young people to succeed academically as a route out of poverty. Dante has just received his A-level results and plans to study at university — an ambition his father shares fiercely. The arrival of baby Emma shatters this plan and exposes how fragile the family’s stability really is.

When Blackman wrote the novel, the UK had one of the highest rates of teen pregnancy in Western Europe. Government campaigns focused heavily on young mothers, but teen fathers were largely invisible in public discussion. Blackman deliberately centres Dante’s experience as a young father — challenging the assumption that parenthood is solely a female concern. The novel asks: what happens to the boy when the baby arrives? This makes Boys Don’t Cry unusual and socially significant.

Masculinity and the Title

The title Boys Don’t Cry is a direct reference to toxic masculinity — the cultural expectation that men and boys should suppress their emotions, never show vulnerability and always appear strong. Both Dante and Adam are trapped by this expectation in different ways. Dante is expected to “man up” and cope with sudden fatherhood without complaint. Adam is expected to hide his sexuality because being gay does not fit the masculine ideal. The title is ironic: the novel shows that boys do cry, and that emotional honesty is a strength, not a weakness.

Key Fact

The title works on two levels: literally, it reflects the societal pressure on Dante and Adam to hide their pain; symbolically, it represents Blackman’s challenge to all forms of prejudice that force people to conceal their true selves.

Dual Narration: Two Brothers, Two Struggles

One of Blackman’s most important structural choices is dual narration. The novel alternates between Dante’s first-person chapters and Adam’s. This structure allows the reader to see the same family from two completely different angles. Dante is consumed by the shock of fatherhood; Adam is consumed by the fear of coming out as gay. Neither brother fully understands what the other is going through, and the reader has access to both inner worlds. This creates dramatic irony — we see connections and parallels that the characters themselves miss.

In Edexcel’s Component 1 Section B, you write a single essay responding to a quotation. You are assessed on AO1 (response and textual references), AO3 (context) and AO4 (SPaG) — but not AO2 (language analysis). This means you should focus on what Blackman shows through her characters and themes, linking consistently to the social context, rather than doing close word-level analysis. However, discussing structural choices like dual narration is valuable because it shows how Blackman shapes the reader’s understanding of prejudice.

Blackman’s Wider Purpose

Blackman is best known for her Noughts & Crosses series, which explores racism through a world where Black people hold power and White people are the oppressed minority. Boys Don’t Cry shares the same underlying concern: how do prejudice and power structures shape the lives of young people? However, while Noughts & Crosses uses speculative fiction to defamiliarise racism, Boys Don’t Cry is set in recognisable, everyday Britain. The prejudices here — against gay teenagers, against young fathers, against families that do not fit the ‘normal’ template — are not fantastical. They are the ones Blackman’s readers encounter in their own schools, homes and communities. This makes the novel feel personal and urgent.

Key Themes at a Glance

The novel weaves together several interconnected themes. Prejudice is the umbrella theme: homophobia, assumptions about teen parents, and gender stereotypes are all forms of prejudice that damage the characters. Closely linked are the themes of family, identity, responsibility and growing up. Every chapter asks, in different ways, the same question: what does it mean to be a man, a father, a brother, a son — when society’s rules make it harder to be yourself?

Key Fact

The five central themes are: masculinity, prejudice and acceptance, family, responsibility and identity. In the exam, you must explore how these themes connect to the social context of modern Britain — this is where AO3 marks come from.

title: Dante's Story: The Baby
content_html:
A-Level Results Day: The Opening

The novel opens on what should be one of the happiest days of Dante’s life. He is seventeen, waiting for his A-level results, and expecting the grades that will take him to university. Blackman immediately establishes the stakes: for Dante and his father, university represents escape — a route to a better life. Dante’s dad, Tyler Senior, has pinned all his hopes on his eldest son’s education. This opening is deliberately charged with tension because the reader senses that something is about to go very wrong.

Key Fact

Blackman opens on A-level results day to establish Dante’s dreams before destroying them. The contrast between his expectations and the reality of Melanie’s arrival creates the novel’s central dramatic conflict within the first few chapters.

Melanie’s Arrival

When the doorbell rings, Dante expects the postman with his results. Instead, his ex-girlfriend Melanie is standing on the doorstep — holding a baby. She tells Dante that the child, Emma, is his daughter. The shock is total. Dante had no idea Melanie was pregnant, and she has kept the baby a secret for months. Melanie does not ask Dante if he wants to be involved; she simply places Emma in his arms and, within a short time, disappears from their lives.

This moment is the novel’s inciting incident. Everything that follows — Dante’s sacrifice, his father’s fury, Adam’s parallel struggle — stems from Melanie placing Emma in Dante’s arms. Blackman gives Melanie very little dialogue or interiority; the reader never fully understands her motivations, which mirrors Dante’s own confusion and helplessness.

Dante’s first reaction is denial. He does not want to believe Emma is his. He tries to convince himself that Melanie is lying, that there has been a mistake. This is a natural psychological response to overwhelming shock, and Blackman presents it with raw honesty. Dante does not immediately become a loving father — he is terrified, angry and desperate to escape. This realism is important: Blackman refuses to sentimentalise teen parenthood or pretend that love is instant. Dante’s journey to acceptance will take the entire novel.

Dad’s Reaction: Fury and Disappointment

Tyler Senior’s reaction to Emma’s arrival is explosive. He is furious — not just at the situation, but at what it means for Dante’s future. Dad has raised two boys alone since their mother left, and he has sacrificed everything for their education. To him, Dante becoming a teen father is a catastrophic failure that will trap his son in the same cycle of poverty and limited opportunity that he has spent years trying to break. His anger is laced with disappointment — and beneath the disappointment, fear.

Key Fact

Dad’s rage at Dante is driven by love, not cruelty. He has spent years as a single parent trying to give his sons a better life. Emma’s arrival represents the collapse of that plan. His emotional response reflects the novel’s title: he expresses fury because expressing fear or sadness would make him vulnerable.

Giving Up University

Perhaps the most painful consequence of Melanie’s arrival is Dante’s realisation that he cannot go to university. Even though he gets the grades he needs, the practicalities of caring for a newborn make it impossible. This is a devastating moment because Blackman has established university as Dante’s only escape route. Giving it up is not a choice made out of nobility — it is forced on him by circumstance. Blackman uses this to explore the social context of social mobility: for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, one unexpected event can close doors permanently.

In modern Britain, university education is often presented as the key to social mobility — the idea that hard work and qualifications allow people to improve their economic situation regardless of their background. However, research consistently shows that young people from lower-income families face more barriers: financial pressure, lack of family support networks, and the impact of unexpected life events. Blackman shows this reality through Dante: he has the ability and the ambition, but a single event derails his path. This is not a failure of character; it is a failure of the support systems around him.

Adam’s Perspective on the Crisis

Through the dual narration, the reader also sees these opening events from Adam’s perspective. While Dante is consumed by the shock of fatherhood, Adam is dealing with his own hidden crisis: he is gay and terrified of telling his family. Adam watches his father’s explosive reaction to Dante’s news and concludes that coming out would provoke an even worse response. The two storylines run in parallel, each intensifying the other. Adam thinks: if Dad cannot accept an unplanned baby, how will he ever accept a gay son?

Key Fact

Adam’s decision to stay closeted is directly influenced by watching Dad’s reaction to Dante. Blackman uses the parallel narratives to show how one form of prejudice (against teen parents) fuels another (Adam’s fear of homophobic rejection).

title: Adam's Story: Coming Out
content_html:
Adam’s Hidden World

While Dante’s chapters deal with the visible crisis of sudden fatherhood, Adam’s chapters reveal a quieter, slower-burning agony. Adam is Dante’s younger brother, still at school, and he is gay. He has known this about himself for some time, but he has told nobody in his family. Through Adam’s interior monologue, Blackman shows the exhausting daily effort of hiding who you are — monitoring every word, every gesture, every reaction — to avoid detection.

Key Fact

Adam’s storyline runs parallel to Dante’s throughout the novel. Both brothers are hiding something: Dante hides his fear about fatherhood; Adam hides his sexuality. Blackman uses this parallel to argue that the pressure to conform — whether to masculine stereotypes or to heteronormativity — damages everyone.

Homophobic Bullying at School

Adam faces persistent bullying at school. Other students suspect or sense that he is different, and they target him with homophobic language and, eventually, physical violence. Blackman does not flinch from showing the reality of this: the casual cruelty of slurs in corridors, the isolation of lunchtime, the constant calculation of which routes are safe. Adam endures this largely in silence because reporting it would mean explaining why he is being targeted — and he is not ready to do that.

This reflects a well-documented reality in British schools. When Blackman published the novel in 2010, studies showed that over 65% of LGBTQ+ students in the UK experienced homophobic bullying. Section 28, a law that had prevented schools from positively discussing homosexuality, was only repealed in 2003. Its legacy lingered: many teachers felt uncertain about how to support LGBTQ+ students, and schools lacked the policies and training to address homophobic bullying effectively.

Section 28 of the Local Government Act 1988 stated that a local authority “shall not intentionally promote homosexuality or publish material with the intention of promoting homosexuality.” Although it was repealed in 2003, its effects were long-lasting. A generation of teachers had been trained in an environment where discussing homosexuality positively was effectively banned. This meant that when Blackman was writing Boys Don’t Cry, many LGBTQ+ teenagers still felt invisible in schools. Adam’s experience — silence, isolation, fear — directly reflects this cultural context.

Josh: Love and Risk

Adam’s relationship with Josh is one of the novel’s most tender and most dangerous threads. Josh is Adam’s boyfriend, and their relationship offers Adam moments of genuine happiness and acceptance. However, it also increases the risk of exposure. Every time they are together in public, Adam is aware that being seen could trigger the bullying he already endures — or worse. Blackman presents their relationship without sensationalising it: they are two teenagers in love, dealing with the same feelings any couple would, but with the added burden of a hostile social environment.

Key Fact

Josh’s character serves a crucial function: he proves that Adam’s sexuality is natural and healthy. Without Josh, Adam’s storyline would only be about suffering. With Josh, Blackman shows that the problem is not Adam’s identity — it is society’s response to it.

The Family’s Reaction

When Adam’s sexuality is eventually revealed, the family’s reaction is complex. Dad does not respond with the immediate acceptance that Adam needs. His initial reaction is one of shock and discomfort — not outright rejection, but not the supportive embrace Adam hoped for either. This is painfully realistic. Blackman avoids the extremes of complete rejection or instant acceptance, instead showing the messy, difficult middle ground where love and prejudice coexist in the same person.

Dante’s response is more straightforward: he is surprised but supportive. Having gone through his own crisis with Emma, Dante has developed empathy — he knows what it feels like to have your life turned upside down and to need your family to stand with you. This is one of Blackman’s most powerful structural choices: Dante’s journey through fatherhood prepares him to be the brother Adam needs.

Blackman deliberately structures the novel so that Dante and Adam face parallel forms of prejudice. Dante is judged for being a teen father; Adam is judged for being gay. Both are expected to feel shame. Both initially hide their truth. Both eventually find that honesty — however painful — is the only path to a genuine life. The dual narration makes these parallels explicit: the reader moves between two brothers trapped by the same cultural forces, even though their specific situations are very different.

Context: Changing Attitudes to Homosexuality

The novel was published in 2010, a time of significant change for LGBTQ+ rights in Britain. Civil partnerships had been legal since 2004, but same-sex marriage would not become law until 2014. Public attitudes were shifting but uneven: opinion polls showed growing acceptance among younger people, while many older generations remained uncomfortable. Blackman captures this transitional moment through Dad — a man who loves his son but whose instinctive reactions are shaped by the less accepting world he grew up in. The novel does not condemn Dad; it shows how prejudice is learned and can be unlearned.

Key Fact

Blackman published Boys Don’t Cry in 2010 — after civil partnerships (2004) but before same-sex marriage (2014). Dad’s struggle to accept Adam reflects this transitional period in British attitudes towards homosexuality.

title: Fatherhood & Sacrifice
content_html:
From Reluctance to Love

Dante’s transformation from a terrified, reluctant teenager to a devoted father is the emotional heart of the novel. Blackman does not rush this process. In the early chapters, Dante resents Emma. He sees her as the obstacle that has destroyed his future — his university place, his freedom, his plans. He does not know how to hold a baby, change a nappy or soothe a crying infant. His first attempts at parenting are clumsy and exhausting. Blackman presents these moments with unflinching honesty, refusing to idealise teen fatherhood.

Key Fact

Dante’s love for Emma does not arrive in a single dramatic moment. It develops gradually through the daily acts of caring: feeding, changing, comforting, staying awake through the night. Blackman shows that love is built through sacrifice, not sentimentality.

Dropping Out of Education

One of the novel’s most painful developments is Dante’s decision to leave education. Even after losing his university place, there is a brief period where he considers alternative paths — resitting, applying later, finding some way to combine study and childcare. But the practical reality is overwhelming. There is no one to look after Emma during the day. Melanie has disappeared. Dad works full time. Aunt Jackie helps when she can, but she has her own life. Dante is, for all practical purposes, a single parent at seventeen.

Blackman uses Dante’s situation to expose a gap in social support. In theory, young parents in Britain have access to education and childcare assistance. In practice, the systems are patchy, underfunded and difficult to navigate — especially for a young man, since most support services are designed with young mothers in mind. Dante falls through the cracks not because he is lazy or irresponsible, but because the infrastructure does not serve him.

When Boys Don’t Cry was published, public discourse about teen pregnancy focused almost exclusively on young mothers. Government campaigns targeted girls; charities and support services were designed for women. Young fathers were either invisible or vilified — portrayed as absent, irresponsible or uninterested. Blackman deliberately challenges this stereotype by making Dante the primary carer. She forces the reader to see teen fatherhood from the inside, and in doing so, exposes the assumptions and prejudices that surround it.

Financial Struggles

Money is a constant pressure in the novel. The Bridgeman family is not wealthy. Dad works hard but earns a modest income. The addition of a baby — nappies, formula, clothes, equipment — stretches their already tight budget. Blackman does not dwell on this with lengthy descriptions of poverty; instead, she weaves financial anxiety into everyday moments. Dante worries about the cost of nappies. Dad frets about heating bills. These details ground the novel in a recognisable social reality and prevent it from becoming abstract or sentimental.

Key Fact

The financial strain on the Bridgeman family reflects the reality of many working-class households in Britain. Blackman shows that poverty is not just about lacking money — it limits choices, increases stress and makes every unexpected event (like a baby) a potential crisis.

Melanie’s Absence

Melanie’s disappearance from the novel is as significant as her initial arrival. After leaving Emma with Dante, she does not return, does not contact them and provides no financial or emotional support. Blackman gives Melanie almost no explanation for her actions. This absence serves multiple purposes. Practically, it forces Dante into the role of sole carer. Thematically, it raises questions about responsibility: is Melanie a victim of her own impossible circumstances, or has she made a selfish choice? Blackman deliberately refuses to answer this, leaving the reader to form their own judgement.

By denying Melanie her own narrative voice, Blackman mirrors the way society often reduces young mothers to a single label: ‘irresponsible’. We never learn Melanie’s full story — her family situation, her mental health, the pressures she faced. This narrative choice challenges the reader: if you judge Melanie harshly, are you doing exactly what the novel warns against — making assumptions based on incomplete information? In the exam, discussing Blackman’s treatment of Melanie shows sophisticated understanding of authorial choices.

The Growing Bond

As weeks pass, Dante’s feelings towards Emma transform. He begins to notice small things: the way she grips his finger, her first smile, the way she calms when she hears his voice. These moments are quiet but powerful. Blackman shows that the bond between parent and child is not automatic — it is built through presence, patience and the daily choice to keep going even when you are exhausted and afraid. By the middle of the novel, Dante can no longer imagine his life without Emma. The university dream has faded; what has replaced it is something he never expected and could not have planned for.

Key Fact

Blackman presents Dante’s love for Emma as earned, not given. He does not love her because she is his daughter; he loves her because he has cared for her. This challenges the stereotype that men are not natural caregivers and reinforces the novel’s message that masculinity can include tenderness and vulnerability.

title: The Climax & Resolution
content_html:
The Violent Climax

The novel’s climax is a moment of sudden, shocking violence. Adam is attacked by a group of boys in a hate crime because of his sexuality. The attack is brutal and unprovoked — a physical expression of the homophobic attitudes that have simmered throughout the novel. Blackman does not shy away from the reality: the language the attackers use, the fear Adam feels, the injuries he sustains. This is the point where the novel’s themes of prejudice and masculinity collide with devastating force.

Key Fact

The homophobic attack on Adam is the novel’s climax — the moment where hidden prejudice becomes visible, physical violence. It forces every character, especially Dad, to confront the real-world consequences of homophobia.

Dante’s Response: Protective Brother

Dante’s reaction to Adam’s attack reveals how much he has changed. The Dante of the opening chapters was consumed by his own crisis — fatherhood, lost dreams, anger. The Dante who responds to Adam’s attack is a different person: protective, empathetic and fierce. He does not hesitate. His instinct is to protect his brother, regardless of the danger to himself. Blackman uses this moment to show that Dante’s experience of caring for Emma has expanded his capacity for love and protectiveness beyond his own child.

Crucially, Dante’s protectiveness is not driven by traditional masculine aggression. He does not seek revenge or violence. Instead, he comforts Adam, takes him home and makes it clear that he accepts him completely. This challenges the masculine ideal that the title references: Dante proves that being a man means protecting through love, not through violence.

The attack on Adam reflects a documented reality. In the years around the novel’s publication, homophobic hate crimes in England and Wales were rising — partly because reporting was increasing, but also because LGBTQ+ people, particularly young people, remained vulnerable to violence. A 2008 Stonewall report found that one in five lesbian and gay people had experienced a homophobic hate crime in the previous three years. Blackman includes this violence not for shock value but to make an urgent social point: prejudice is not just about words and attitudes. It has physical, sometimes life-threatening consequences.

Dad’s Turning Point

The attack on Adam is also the moment that breaks through Dad’s defences. Throughout the novel, Dad has expressed his discomfort with Adam’s sexuality through silence and avoidance. He has not been overtly cruel, but he has not been supportive either. Seeing his son physically hurt because of who he is forces Dad to make a choice: will he remain trapped in his own discomfort, or will he put his child first? Dad chooses his son. This does not happen through a dramatic speech or an instant transformation — Blackman shows it through small, practical acts of care and a gradual softening of his manner.

Key Fact

Dad’s acceptance of Adam after the attack demonstrates Blackman’s key message: prejudice is not permanent. People can change when confronted with the human cost of their attitudes. Dad’s journey mirrors the broader shift in British society towards LGBTQ+ acceptance.

The Family Comes Together

The novel’s resolution is cautiously hopeful. The Bridgeman family does not suddenly become perfect. Dad is still awkward. Dante is still exhausted. Adam is still healing. But they are together, and they are honest with each other for the first time. Emma has, in an unexpected way, brought them closer — her presence forced Dante to grow up, and his growth gave him the empathy to support Adam. The family unit, battered and imperfect, survives because its members choose each other.

Blackman’s ending refuses the extremes of tragedy or fairy tale. There is no triumphant final scene where every problem is solved. Instead, there is a quiet sense that things will be difficult but manageable — that this family has the love and resilience to face whatever comes next. This restraint is one of the novel’s great strengths: it treats its characters, and its readers, as intelligent enough to accept complexity.

The novel ends with a sense of qualified hope. Blackman does not promise that everything will be fine. Adam still lives in a society where homophobia exists. Dante still faces the challenges of single parenthood without a degree. Dad still has work to do on his attitudes. But the fact that they have survived their worst moments together — and that honesty has replaced secrecy — suggests that the family is stronger than the forces ranged against it. This is Blackman’s most politically significant message: prejudice can be overcome, but it requires courage, honesty and the willingness to change.

Structural Significance of the Climax

The placement of the attack near the novel’s end is a deliberate structural choice. Blackman spends most of the novel building both storylines — Dante’s fatherhood and Adam’s hidden identity — as parallel but separate crises. The attack is the point where they converge. It forces every character to respond simultaneously: Dante must be a brother; Dad must be a father; the family must function as a unit. Everything that has come before — every lesson Dante has learned from Emma, every silence Adam has endured — is tested in this single moment.

Key Fact

The climax brings the novel’s two parallel narratives together for the first time. Dante’s growth through fatherhood has prepared him to support Adam; Adam’s suffering forces the family to confront its avoidance. The dual narration structure pays off at this moment because the reader understands both perspectives fully.

title: Character Analysis
content_html:
Characters as Vehicles for Theme

In Boys Don’t Cry, every character serves Blackman’s thematic purpose. No one exists simply to fill a role in the plot — each character embodies or challenges a specific social attitude. Understanding how characters function thematically is essential for the Edexcel exam, where you must connect your analysis to the novel’s context. In this lesson, we examine each major character and what they represent.

Dante Bridgeman

Dante is the novel’s primary protagonist and its moral centre. At seventeen, he is intelligent, ambitious and focused on escaping his background through education. When Melanie arrives with Emma, Dante’s defining characteristic becomes his willingness — however reluctant — to take responsibility. His character arc moves from resentment and denial to acceptance and deep love. Blackman uses Dante to challenge the stereotype that young men are incapable of nurturing, showing that fatherhood transforms him into someone more empathetic, more patient and more courageous than the boy he was at the beginning.

Key Fact

Dante’s most important quality is his capacity for growth. He begins the novel defined by ambition; he ends it defined by love. Blackman shows that being a ‘real man’ is not about toughness or success — it is about showing up for the people who need you.

Adam Bridgeman

Adam is Dante’s younger brother and the novel’s second narrator. Where Dante’s crisis is visible and public (a baby cannot be hidden), Adam’s crisis is internal and secret. He is gay, and he spends most of the novel terrified of being discovered. Adam is perceptive, sensitive and deeply aware of the attitudes around him. He watches his father’s reactions carefully, calculating whether honesty is safe. Through Adam, Blackman gives a voice to the thousands of LGBTQ+ teenagers who navigate school, family and society while hiding a fundamental part of who they are.

Adam’s chapters provide the reader with information that Dante does not have, creating dramatic irony. We know Adam is suffering while Dante is absorbed in his own problems. This irony deepens both storylines: Dante’s ignorance of Adam’s pain makes his eventual support more powerful, and Adam’s observation of Dante’s crisis explains why he remains silent about his own.

Dad (Tyler Bridgeman Senior)

Dad is one of Blackman’s most complex and nuanced characters. He is a single father who has raised two boys alone after their mother left. He works hard, values education and wants a better life for his sons. These are admirable qualities. However, Dad also struggles with emotional expression — his love comes out as pressure and control, and his fear manifests as anger. When he learns about Emma, he explodes. When he learns about Adam, he retreats into uncomfortable silence. In both cases, his reaction is rooted in love that he cannot articulate.

Key Fact

Dad embodies the novel’s title more than anyone. He is a man who has been taught that boys don’t cry — that emotional vulnerability is weakness. His journey towards accepting both sons mirrors the broader cultural shift Blackman advocates: that real strength lies in openness, not stoicism.

Emma

Emma is a baby and therefore has no dialogue or agency. Yet she is the novel’s most powerful catalyst. Her arrival destroys Dante’s plans but ultimately transforms him into a better, more empathetic person. Emma’s presence also exposes the family’s fault lines: Dad’s rigidity, the financial pressure, the absence of support. Symbolically, Emma represents new beginnings and the possibility of breaking the cycle — she is the next generation, and how Dante raises her will determine whether the prejudices of the past are repeated or overcome.

Melanie

Melanie is a deliberately underdeveloped character. She appears, leaves Emma, and disappears. Blackman gives her almost no interiority, no backstory and no explanation. This is a conscious authorial choice: by denying Melanie a voice, Blackman forces the reader to confront their own tendency to judge young mothers. If you find yourself calling Melanie ‘selfish’ or ‘irresponsible’, the novel asks you to consider: what pressures was she under? What were her options? The absence of answers is the point.

Josh is Adam’s boyfriend and the novel’s primary symbol of acceptance and normality. His presence proves that Adam’s sexuality is natural and healthy — the problem lies with society, not with Adam. Josh also represents risk: their public relationship makes Adam a target.

Aunt Jackie is the family’s most reliable source of practical and emotional support. She steps in to help with Emma when Dad and Dante are overwhelmed. In a novel full of characters who struggle to communicate, Aunt Jackie represents what a functional support network looks like.

Collette is a girl Dante becomes interested in after Melanie’s departure. She is significant because she accepts Dante despite his situation — proving that being a teen father does not make him unlovable. Collette represents the possibility of a future that includes both Emma and romantic happiness.

Key Fact

Every character in Boys Don’t Cry serves Blackman’s purpose of challenging prejudice. Dante challenges assumptions about teen fathers. Adam challenges homophobia. Dad challenges the idea that older generations cannot change. Melanie challenges the reader’s own tendency to judge without evidence.

title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Themes: The Backbone of Your Essay

For a modern-text essay, the question will focus on a character, theme, relationship or event. Whatever the question, your answer will always need to engage with the novel’s key themes. This lesson examines each theme in detail and provides guidance on how to write about them under exam conditions. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact assessment objectives that will be marked — some modern-text essays focus on response to text and context rather than close language analysis, so make sure you know what is being rewarded before you plan your essay.

Theme 1: Masculinity

Masculinity is the novel’s overarching theme, embedded in the title itself. Blackman explores what society tells boys and men they should be: strong, unemotional, self-reliant, heterosexual, successful. Every major character is constrained by these expectations. Dante is expected to cope with fatherhood without showing fear. Adam is expected to be straight. Dad is expected to hold the family together without expressing vulnerability. The novel’s argument is that this version of masculinity — often called toxic masculinity — damages everyone it touches.

Key Fact

The title Boys Don’t Cry is both a cultural phrase enforcing emotional suppression and an ironic challenge: the novel proves that boys do cry, and that emotional honesty is the foundation of healthy relationships and genuine strength.

Theme 2: Prejudice and Acceptance

Blackman explores multiple forms of prejudice: homophobia (against Adam), stereotyping of teen parents (against Dante), and gender-based assumptions (against both brothers). Her central argument is that prejudice stems from fear and ignorance, not from rational judgement. Dad’s discomfort with Adam’s sexuality is rooted in fear of the unknown, not in hatred. The school bullies attack Adam because his existence challenges their worldview. Blackman shows that acceptance is possible but requires courage: courage to be honest (Adam), courage to stay (Dante), and courage to change (Dad).

To earn strong context marks, you must connect the novel’s themes to the real world. For prejudice, reference: the legacy of Section 28 (repealed 2003) creating a culture of silence in schools; the timeline of LGBTQ+ rights in Britain (civil partnerships 2004, marriage equality 2014); the stigmatisation of teen parents in media and government policy; Blackman’s own experience as a Black British author challenging prejudice through diverse representation. The strongest responses embed context within analysis, not in separate paragraphs.

Theme 3: Family

The Bridgeman family does not fit the ‘traditional’ model: there is no mother, the father is emotionally reserved, one son is a teen parent, and the other is gay. Blackman deliberately constructs this family to challenge the idea that only ‘normal’ families are functional. The novel argues that family is defined by loyalty, love and the willingness to support each other through crisis — not by fitting a template. By the end, the Bridgemans are stronger because of their imperfections, not despite them.

Key Fact

The absent mother is never fully explained. Her departure shaped Dad’s emotional guardedness and forced him into the role of sole carer. When Dante becomes a single parent himself, the parallel is unmistakable: Blackman suggests that the cycle can be broken, but only through conscious effort.

Theme 4: Responsibility

Responsibility is tested from the novel’s opening page. Melanie transfers responsibility to Dante. Dante must accept responsibility for Emma. Dad feels responsible for his sons’ futures. Adam takes responsibility for his own identity by coming out. Blackman explores how responsibility can be forced (Dante’s fatherhood), avoided (Melanie’s disappearance) or embraced (Dad’s eventual acceptance). The novel suggests that taking responsibility — even when you did not choose it — is a defining act of maturity.

Theme 5: Identity and Growing Up

Both Dante and Adam are in the process of discovering who they are. Dante’s identity shifts from ‘ambitious student’ to ‘young father’. Adam’s identity as a gay teenager is something he knows but cannot express. Blackman explores identity as something that is both personal (how you see yourself) and social (how others see you). The novel argues that genuine identity can only emerge through honesty — and that the courage to be honest is the truest form of growing up.

A strong theme essay follows this structure:

Introduction — Respond directly to the prompt and question. State your argument in one or two sentences. Briefly reference the novel’s context.

Main paragraphs (3–4) — Each paragraph should make one clear point, supported by a reference to the text (a quotation if you can remember one, or a specific event/moment), and linked to context. Use the Point-Evidence-Explain-Context (PEEC) structure: make a point, provide evidence from the novel, explain what it shows, and connect it to the wider world.

Conclusion — Return to the prompt. Summarise your argument. End with a final contextual link — why does this matter beyond the novel?

Key Fact

In a closed-book exam, you do not need long quotations. Short, memorable phrases work just as well: ‘the title itself functions as a thesis statement for the entire novel’. You can also use detailed references to events: ‘when Melanie places Emma in Dante’s arms’ is as effective as a direct quotation if you explain its significance.

Exam Command Words

Essay questions use specific command words. The most common are:

‘To what extent do you agree?’ — You must argue a clear position but consider both sides. Do not sit on the fence: state whether you mostly agree or disagree, then explore the counterargument.

‘How does Blackman present...?’ — Focus on what she shows through characters, events and structure. Check your exam board’s mark scheme to see whether close language analysis is rewarded or whether the focus is on whole-text response and context.

‘Explore the significance of...’ — Explain why something matters — to the characters, to the themes, and to the reader’s understanding of the novel’s message.
